turns.response_html:
Moving from a wired camera to a solar-powered setup is a significant shift in how your security system operates. While it offers total freedom of placement, it changes the "high quality" recording experience you're used to because of power management.

If you decide to go this route, the Wyze Battery Cam Pro is the primary choice, as it is specifically designed to work with the Wyze Solar Panel.

Key Differences to Consider

While your current camera likely records continuously or has very long "event" clips because it’s plugged into a wall, solar/battery cameras have to be more conservative to save energy.

FeatureWired Wyze Cam (Current)Wyze Battery Cam Pro + Solar
Power SourcePermanent wall outletRemovable battery + Solar trickle charge
ResolutionUsually 1080p2K HDR (Higher detail than your current cam)
Recording ModeContinuous recording possibleEvent-based only (to save battery)
PlacementLimited by cord lengthAnywhere with 3+ hours of direct sun
Night VisionIR or StarlightColor Night Vision + Built-in Spotlight

Tips for a Solar Setup

  1. Direct Sunlight is Critical: The solar panel needs roughly 3–4 hours of direct, unshaded sunlight per day to keep the battery topped off. If you place it under a deep eave or on the north side of a building, the battery will eventually die.
  2. The "Trail Cam" Logic: Battery cameras use a PIR (Passive Infrared) sensor to "wake up" when they sense heat/motion. This means there is a tiny delay (milliseconds) before it starts recording compared to a wired camera that is "always on."
  3. Winter Performance: In extremely cold climates, lithium batteries charge much slower. You might find yourself needing to manually charge the battery once or twice during the darkest winter months.
  4. MicroSD Support: The Battery Cam Pro still supports local storage (up to 256GB), so you can keep your recordings off the cloud just like your current setup.

Compatibility Note

If you have an older Wyze Cam Outdoor (v1 or v2), those also support solar, but they require a "Base Station" plugged into your router. The Battery Cam Pro is generally preferred now because it connects directly to your Wi-Fi without needing that extra hub.

Are you looking to place this new camera in a spot that gets plenty of sun, or is it a high-traffic area like a front door?

turns.prompt_text: Our entire South sledding glass door gets good Sun Attached 1 file. - 1ebbddbb-7779-4e57-b753-7b9bc8b3e941
turns.response_html:
That looks like a prime spot for a solar-powered setup. Since that sliding door faces south and clearly gets plenty of direct light, a solar panel mounted nearby would likely stay at 100% battery almost year-round without you ever needing to touch it.

Given your setup, there are a few clever ways to handle the mounting:

Mounting Options

  • Glass Mount: You can actually get suction-cup mounts for small solar panels. If you don't want to drill into the exterior of the building, you could stick the panel directly to the upper corner of that glass pane.
  • Frame Mount: Since the door frame is right there, you could use a gutter mount or a small adhesive bracket on the exterior trim to position the panel so it doesn't obstruct your view.
  • Window Sill: If you prefer to keep everything inside, some people have success placing the panel on the interior side of the glass. Just keep in mind that modern "Low-E" glass coatings can reduce solar efficiency by 20% to 30%, so it might charge a bit slower than it would outside.

A Few "Pro" Considerations

  • Cable Management: Wyze solar panels usually come with about 13 feet of cable. Since you’re already used to running micro-USB, you could tuck the thin solar cable along the weather stripping of the door for a very clean, "stealth" install.
  • The "Shadow" Factor: Make sure the panel is high enough so that those parked cars or the roof overhang don't cast a shadow on it during the peak midday sun. Even a small shadow across one corner of a solar panel can significantly drop its power output.

With that much southern exposure, are you thinking of mounting the camera itself inside looking out, or placing it outside to cover the parking area?
